items.summary: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" over the record amount he spent backing Republicans in the US midterms, following sweeping Democratic victories. As the election's top individual donor, Musk gave $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, with much of the spending concentrated in Texas, where many of his companies are based. Speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference for business and political leaders, Musk also said he was "not Maga," describing it as blind adherence to a set of Republican policies that he did not share. The midterms were seen as a bruising defeat for Trump amid pressure over his impact on US living costs, with Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress after flipping swing seats and making historic gains in long-standing Republican areas. Musk acknowledged the heavy losses could affect him and his businesses: incoming Democratic majorities have pledged greater scrutiny of tech firms, including over controversial data centres, while a newly elected Democrat governor in Georgia promised to limit their rollout and associated tax breaks. Lawmakers also suggested SpaceX should be investigated after gaining an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump's re-election. Musk conceded he did not see much return from the spending but added that candidates would likely have fared worse without it. The results are significant for Texas specifically, where Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat after Musk had reportedly spent at least $45m supporting him; SpaceX operates data centres there too. Musk characterized Texas's new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated three-decade-long Republican control by beating Governor Greg Abbott, as "quite moderate," adding that he did not think she was far-left and expected things to be fine in the state under her leadership.
items.title: Musk regrets record midterm spending after Republican defeats

items.summary: Monetary Authority of Singapore managing director Chia Der Jiun warned consumers to avoid giving artificial intelligence agents their financial account login credentials, citing insufficient safeguards to ensure such tools act safely and within users' instructions. Speaking at the Singapore Fintech Festival on Nov 19, he noted that some payment service providers and financial institutions are building agent interfaces into their offerings, while many have yet to establish terms or channels for agents to access financial services. Chia raised concerns about accountability, asking who bears responsibility if an agent transacts incorrectly or beyond its instructions, since the institution cannot always confirm whether it is acting with full customer authorisation. He said a trusted protocol and secure channel are needed for AI agents to access financial services, drawing on lessons from the first phase of MAS' Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) initiative. Those include giving agents sufficient autonomy while operating within clearly defined boundaries, establishing their identities and authority to act on behalf of users, and specifying instructions along with any limits and conditions. Chia stated that the greater an agent's discretion and impact, the stronger the assurance and controls required. As part of a new phase of SAFR, MAS will develop a common "know your agent" protocol for trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions, providing details on who the agent is, whom it represents, its authority, mandate, origins and reliability so that institutions can determine permitted terms and scope and establish a dedicated secure channel. Separately, MAS will set up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute to bring together AI agents and programmable money across two use cases: corporate treasury management, where banks could allow an agent to monitor liquidity positions and due payments, decide when and where funds move, and execute permitted actions using tokenised deposits; and payment services, where customer agents could execute instructions using digital money such as tokenised deposits or stablecoins. In both cases, companies would set the mandates while participating banks would apply controls before executing transactions. Chia said these use cases would provide lessons on the benefits and safeguards of such transactions, adding that consumers and businesses must retain meaningful control over their agents' objectives, mandate and actions, with autonomy bounded and outcomes accountable.
items.title: MAS Chief Warns Against Sharing Financial Login Details With AI Agents

Australian employment fell for a second straight month in October, dropping by 43,500 from September when it had already fallen by a revised 36,400. The combined two-month decline of about 80,000 jobs was the largest such total over five years and far below analysts' forecast of roughly a 25,000 job gain; the October losses were driven mostly by part-time positions. The unemployment rate rose to 4.9%, its highest since October 2021, up from 4.7% the prior month, reaching a level the Reserve Bank of Australia had not expected until late next year when economists had anticipated it holding steady. Krishna Bhimavarapu of State Street Investment Management noted that after higher rates first pressured housing and other rate-sensitive sectors, the slowdown was now appearing clearly in the labour market, strengthening the case that policy is gaining traction and raising the hurdle for another near-term hike.

The soft data bolstered expectations that interest rates have peaked. After five increases in 2026 lifted the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85%, markets stopped pricing in further rises and began expecting lower rates in the second half of 2027, with about 46 basis points of easing now priced by year-end, double what had been expected before data released on November 19. Citi Australia analysts said that with risks to both unemployment and inflation forecasts skewed softer, they expect the RBA to hold at 4.85% until Q3 2027 when it could begin moving back toward neutral, while acknowledging a residual risk of another hike.

The reaction hit currency and bond markets: the Australian dollar fell about 0.5% as it reached an 11-month low of 66.80 US cents, though this was described in the source as its tenth-lowest level over ten months; three-year government bond futures rallied 15 ticks to 95.41, their highest since late August.

Broader labour-market weakness accompanied the headline figures: the participation rate dipped from 66.8% to 66.6%, hours worked fell by 0.2%, and youth unemployment for those aged 15 to 24 rose to 11.3% from 11.1%, its highest in five years. Anecdotal evidence of wider layoffs is building, including a union report that David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs after entering administration on November 18, joining other job losses at Australian firms as the economy slows.

The source carries an AI-generated label and includes anecdotal elements such as the David Jones collapse and RBA board members' private risk warnings. The dollar's level is reported with some ambiguity regarding whether it was its tenth-lowest over ten months or fell to a new low of 66.80 US cents.
items.title: Australia's jobless rate hits five-year high as markets price 2027 rate cuts

items.summary: At The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Elon Musk elaborated on his disapproval of Nvidia's board decision to remove founder and CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about a series of extramarital affairs. Comparing Huang to Michael Jordan, Musk said ousting him is like 'kicking Michael Jordan off your team' when the company was winning, arguing it would not be good for shareholders. He called Huang one of history's most talented entrepreneur-CEOs and stated he would hire him himself if asked about his X post. Musk also signed a petition with over 200,000 other people urging Nvidia to reinstate its former CEO, though the board confirmed it has no plans to bring Huang back. He emphasized that there is no one who can replace Huang, citing decades of relationships and personal loyalty from employees who have declined higher offers elsewhere. Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey echoed this view, saying 'China wants Jensen out,' while noting the decision knocked a trillion dollars off Nvidia's market cap. Musk did not express concern over what Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy could mean for U.S. national security, stating he does not think Huang is disloyal to the United States. Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman reaffirmed their faith in Nvidia to move forward without its 33-year founder-CEO, with Nadella expressing confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.
items.title: Musk Defends Jensen Huang's Ousting at DealBook Summit

items.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella commented on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation, which followed a series of controversies. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Nadella described the situation as tragic and said he wanted to give Huang space to figure things out after their long relationship. Huang stepped down last week from a role he had held for 33 years that was central to Nvidia's rise to one of the world's most valuable companies. His leadership came under scrutiny after reports emerged that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing, as well as affairs with two Nvidia employees, including a direct report. Despite these developments, Nadella said he still has confidence in Nvidia and its close partnership with Microsoft. He pointed to Colette Kress, the interim CEO who worked at Microsoft for a long time, noting that he remains connected to the same people he dealt with before Huang's departure and trusts the team to continue doing good work. Nadella also reflected on how founders like Bill Gates built larger-than-life personas as CEOs but are not gods, observing that companies must eventually have someone take over when they need to succeed.
items.title: Nadella expresses confidence in Nvidia amid Huang's departure

The Nutrient Data Extraction API (formerly PSPDFKit) addresses errors where large language models present wrong document values as fact. It parses PDFs, scans, images and Office files into spatial JSON or Markdown, mapping fields from a document onto the user's JSON schema through split, classify and form endpoints that serve as building blocks for document pipelines. Each extracted value is anchored to a page via a bounding box, receives a match label and a confidence score. Nutrient runs on its cloud API, self-hosted servers through an SDK or an Apple silicon Mac app.

The service offers four parse modes plus auto routing; when the mode is omitted it defaults to understand. Auto routes each page among structure, understand and agentic modes. Testing happens in Studio, a browser workspace for configuring parsing, extraction, classification, splitting and form filling on sample files before writing code. A typical loop uploads a document, drafts or generates a schema, runs it against fresh documents while inspecting values and citations, then saves the setup as a versioned preset called a processor with a proc_ ID; presets can be scored against up to 25 reviewed documents in an evaluation set.

On Nutrient's WholeDoc Bench parsing score of 86.2 on 5 November 2026 is not extraction accuracy, and extract adds $0.006 per page. The agentic setting tops the leaderboard at 86.2 for 1.8¢ per page versus 67.1 at 17.8¢ for the best frontier-model setting.

Grounded confidence combines optional signals of token probability, candidate margin, grounding and format; Nutrient's NLI grounding model is open under Apache-2.0. A grounded value can still answer the wrong field, so each field also receives a match label of id_match, id_match_multiblock, id_match_partial, fuzzy_match or not_found, which should be gated on before confidence. When no score exists, confidence is omitted rather than low.

Pricing uses dollars from one balance shared across Nutrient's cloud APIs; the free plan gives $5 monthly covering about 330 understand-mode extractions, Starter costs $75 for $90 of usage and Growth costs $275 for $345. Understand-mode extraction runs at $15 per 1,000 pages while agentic parsing is $0.018 per page.

Nutrient's document decision model powers classify and split; the company reports a 96.2% split F1 against 63.7% for Typesafe AI's Jev. The hosted MCP server needs no API key, with Claude Code connecting in one command while Claude and Codex also work via OAuth.

Nutrient built and ran WholeDoc Bench across 480 documents, 30+ languages and seven areas; the code is Apache-2.0 with a 10-document public sample but the main test set remains private. Cross-page continuity is described as the biggest gap: on 44 documents with page-spanning tables, 15 of 19 settings rarely kept them whole, and charts remain hard at a best WholeDoc chart score of 64.5.

The demo covers flat schemas only; production needs type and business-rule checks beyond the illustrative 0.97 confidence bar used for money fields in Nutrient's mortgage tutorial.
items.title: Nutrient Data Extraction API: Grounded JSON Parsing With Citations and Confidence

items.summary: The Trump administration announced new measures this week that make it more difficult for Chinese companies to obtain some of the world's most advanced AI chips. For years, firms such as Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from overseas data centers, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally barred from physically importing into China through a practice known as remote access. Under plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers wishing to supply large amounts of computing power to China will now need special licenses and face additional regulatory burdens. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where officials suspect significant smuggling has occurred. These measures are not new policy ideas; similar proposals have circulated in Washington for some time. However, the timing of Monday's announcement coincides with a scandal involving Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO last week after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence services and previously employed at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company linked to chip smuggling. A White House spokesperson told WIRED that the new rule would "crack down on the smuggling of advanced US chips" and help ensure America's most advanced chips go first to American innovators rather than Chinese shell companies. The restrictions trace their origins to fall 2022, when the Biden administration introduced rules designed to limit China's access to advanced AI chips and related manufacturing equipment. The strategy relied on restricting chip exports while American firms like Nvidia dominated the market for training hardware. Enforcement has fallen to the Bureau of Industry and Security within the Commerce Department, which had a budget of just $235 million in 2026. Megaspeed has become a prominent example of smuggling concerns at BIS, though it is not the only company suspected of involvement or necessarily the largest. According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of an estimated 136,000 AI chips that Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 were unaccounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips. Historically, Chinese companies did not need to physically import chips; they could rent overseas data center capacity without violating US export controls. Analysts had argued that allowing such access kept Chinese firms dependent on American technology and discouraged domestic alternatives, though restricting the practice would be difficult to enforce and could harm US chipmakers. Monday's announcement marks a shift toward regulating how Chinese companies use American technology even when hardware never enters China. Evidence suggests export controls have made it harder for Chinese AI companies to match their American competitors' computing power, but assessing the precise impact remains difficult. The restrictions have imposed costs on American suppliers: a Federal Reserve Bank of New York study estimated that earlier US export restrictions wiped $130 billion from affected companies' combined market value while hurting profitability and employment. China has responded by pursuing alternatives such as Huawei's megachip systems linking powerful chips together, and the DeepSeek lab demonstrated that improved training efficiency can yield competitive models with fewer resources.
items.title: Trump administration tightens controls on China's access to advanced AI chips

items.summary: Prof Caroline Mitchell of Keele University, writing as a GP in Sheffield, argues that software built for the fragmented US insurance-based system does not fit the universal public service model of the NHS. She notes that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature within the UK context because they were developed primarily for an entirely different healthcare environment. To illustrate this mismatch, she cites a consultant who described managing seven bolt-on software systems across a single consultation, one focused on billing functions, and contrasts it with a senior US hospital administrator's view that most American health data systems exist mainly to record care for reimbursement. She emphasizes that NHS general practice records are designed to support lifelong patient care and safe prescribing rather than tracking insurance allowances consumed during the year, pointing out how astounded her colleague was by this difference in purpose. Mitchell also questions why the NHS should rely on a US firm to manage its data when the UK has demonstrated healthcare-software innovation of its own, specifically citing Emis, developed with GP leadership, which transformed primary care IT decades ago. She concludes that software built for an insurance market may simply not be the best fit for universal healthcare systems.
items.title: Letter arguing Palantir is ill-suited to NHS healthcare

items.summary: After a quiet period following his 2008 departure from EA and Maxis, Will Wright is promoting his next project, MyMems, which uses generative AI to build a game-like experience from players' memories. The title is slated for release next year and comes from Wright's Gallium Studios in partnership with Artificial Agency. According to the studio's press release, MyMems differentiates itself by 'turn[ing] the simulation inward,' mining player-provided memories to create digital people who form teams to solve puzzles within the game world. Wright illustrates this concept with examples such as imagining a Grand Slam match between his grandmother and Serena Williams, or selecting three real-life contacts to help build a bridge across a chasm. He noted that The Sims' 'plausible behavior' failed to capture real-life nuances like claustrophobia or family conflict, prompting the shift toward personalizing games using actual memories and experiences of people players know. Wright said MyMems will extract generalized themes from memories into self-contained zones he compared to theme park areas, with sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths each potentially forming their own playable sections. Players can also create worlds based on shared memories involving family, friends, and co-workers.
items.title: Will Wright's AI memory-based simulation MyMems

items.summary: Ukrainian authorities, working with the FBI, arrested four suspected members of an international ransomware organization linked to more than $40.5 million in ransom payments from at least 28 companies worldwide. The arrests followed a two-year investigation into a cybercrime group comprising at least 27 individuals from Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Russia, and other countries, which was connected to a larger network of more than 60 members across eight jurisdictions that included former Conti gang members. According to acting National Police chief Maksym Tsutskiridze speaking with Censor.NET, the organization targeted companies in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, logistics, and financial sectors as well as critical infrastructure. Investigators said attackers researched victims' finances, assets, employees, and IT vulnerabilities before launching attacks designed to steal data, encrypt systems, and extort cryptocurrency payments. Tsutskiridze stated that at least 28 companies transferred more than $40.5 million in ransoms, equivalent to approximately UAH 1.8 billion, noting this was money already paid while the full extent of damage remained under assessment. Court records identify Warren Oil Company as a victim of an August 2024 attack in which hackers copied 1.4 TB of data before receiving an 84.5 BTC ransom payment equivalent to approximately $5 million at the time, and describe how attackers initially demanded $10 million but ultimately received $5 million after negotiations. Records also allege Newpark Resources paid $1.5 million in December 2024 while Quantum Health paid $5 million in June 2026 following an initial $15 million ransom demand. LeMagIT reported that the BlackSuit gang claimed Maxxis International as a victim in November 2024, and Ukrainian court records identify Chaos as the ransomware used by the organization. The Conti operation shut down in May 2022 with members dispersing into smaller gangs including BlackSuit, which operated first as Quantum ransomware before becoming Royal and then BlackSuit after high-profile attacks such as one against Dallas, Texas. However, Ukrainian authorities have not identified the four arrested suspects as former Conti members or confirmed their individual affiliations with BlackSuit or Chaos. To breach corporate networks, attackers impersonated IT support personnel using a custom platform with AI-generated voice messages to automate fraudulent calls that tricked employees into disclosing login credentials or installing remote-access software; in one incident an attacker kept an employee on the phone while another accessed systems until intrusion was confirmed. Court records describe additional tactics including phishing pages impersonating corporate VPN services, spoofed phone numbers, and tools such as TeamViewer and AnyDesk, with attackers obtaining two-factor authentication codes to gain network access during the Warren Oil attack before stealing information and encrypting files. Tsutskiridze explained that victims were pressured from both sides by data encryption and threats to publish stolen information, forcing cryptocurrency ransom payments. Ukrainian authorities conducted 66 simultaneous searches across Kyiv and 11 regions of Ukraine as part of the joint operation with U.S. law enforcement; four suspected key members were detained though their exact arrest locations were not disclosed. During these searches investigators seized computers, mobile phones, bank cards, nearly $370,000 in cash, and €20,000. The suspects face charges related to participating in a criminal organization and unauthorized interference with information systems under Ukrainian law, carrying up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Authorities say the investigation is ongoing as they work to identify additional members of the international network and their involvement in other cyberattacks, while also releasing investigative video footage including raids, seized cash, interviews, suspect questioning, and audio from an alleged extortion call demanding $15 million after claiming to have stolen more than 1.5 TB of corporate data.
items.title: Ukraine and FBI Arrest Ransomware Gang Members Linked to $40M in Ransoms

The article reports that despite billions of dollars in government funding over recent years, North America has barely increased its ability to process heavy rare earths into defense-grade metals and magnets. MP Materials received more than $1 billion in combined financing, USA Rare Earth secured a $1.6 billion government financing package, and the Department of Defense and Department of Energy have funded pilot programs, feasibility studies, and demonstration projects across the sector. China still controls approximately 90% of global rare earth processing and produces nearly every ounce of dysprosium and terbium used in magnets powering American weapons systems.

On November 3, the U.S. Army signed a nonbinding term sheet with REalloys (Nasdaq: ALOY) to develop heavy rare earth processing at Tooele Army Depot in Utah. The deal covers approximately 200 acres, includes a potential 75-year lease and a right of first offer on production, and requires no government equity, taxpayer-funded construction, or grant money. REalloys will finance and build the facility while the Army provides land and security perimeter; REalloys pays fair-market rent and the Army receives participation rent once commercial operations begin.

Jeff Waksman, the Army's principal deputy assistant secretary for installations, energy and environment, said the arrangement lets the Army expand the critical minerals industrial base without putting taxpayer dollars at risk. The article notes that rare earth metallization is identified by the Center for Strategic and International Studies as the least developed and most difficult capability to rebuild outside China, requiring years of operational expertise rather than capital alone.

The Tooele model aligns incentives through a participation rent structure so REalloys must make economics work on its own. The Army would be first in line to purchase material before any other buyer but still has its own procurement process. In March 2026, the company won a Defense Logistics Agency contract to develop modular metallization technology for samarium and gadolinium.

The article states that REalloys' Euclid, Ohio facility holds an exclusive 80% offtake on production from the Saskatchewan Research Council's rare earth processing facility, which was designed without Chinese technology. The SRC facility targets annual capacity of approximately 525 tonnes of NdPr metal, 30 tonnes of dysprosium oxide, and 15 tonnes of terbium oxide, with initial NdPr metallization capacity targeted for commissioning in Q1 2027.

In September 2026, REalloys appointed Dr. Muhammad Imran as Chief Operating Officer; the article states he is a former CTO of SRC with 17 years of rare earth processing experience and built the SRC processing technology. The company has secured feedstock agreements spanning Saskatchewan, Wyoming, Appalachia, Kazakhstan, Brazil, and Greenland, including a 15-year offtake for 15% of Phase 1 production from Critical Metals' Tanbreez project.

The article states that at full scale REalloys envisions the largest heavy rare earth metallization facility in the Western world. On January 1, 2027, expanded Pentagon procurement rules take effect restricting Chinese-origin rare earth materials in American weapons systems; Beijing suspended its own export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements only until January 10, 2027.

The article states that REalloys is qualifying defense-grade materials ahead of the deadline with high-purity rare earth materials expected from SRC as early as Q4 2026. Evolution Metals & Technologies Corp. (Nasdaq: EMAT) is expanding its plant in Pohang, South Korea toward annual capacity above 10,000 metric tons; on October 31 the company raised fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to $10 million to $11 million while keeping a fiscal 2027 target of $400 million to $460 million.

The article states that Evolution's outlook is not based on contracted volumes and lists its ability to continue as a going concern among the risks. Perpetua Resources (Nasdaq: PPTA) received up to $40 million over 36 months from the Army's Defense Ordnance Technology Consortium for tungsten exploration at its Stibnite project in Idaho, matched by Perpetua with only about $18 million committed; on November 13 it reported $443.4 million in unrestricted cash while its $2.9 billion EXIM loan is not expected to close until the first quarter of 2027.

The article states that REalloys closed an approximately $100 million institutional private placement in June 2026 and reported $122.4 million in cash with virtually no debt; its leadership includes Chairman Stephen S. DuMont, President of GM Defense General Jack Keane (Ret.), and former Secretary of Defense Chief of Staff Joe Kasper.

Lithium Americas (NYSE: LAC) raised its Thacker Pass Phase 1 capital estimate to $3.83 billion from $2.93 billion on November 11, citing labor costs, added contingency, and tariffs; the article states it targets mechanical completion in late 2027.

Albemarle (NYSE: ALB) reported net sales of $1.55 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $646 million up 186% from a year earlier on November 4, with Energy Storage prices averaging $20.02 per kilogram of lithium carbonate equivalent; the article states it cut 2026 capital spending guidance to $300 million to $350 million from about $500 million.

The article concludes that if the Tooele model works, it could become a template where the federal government provides land, security, and demand while the private sector supplies capital, technology, and operational expertise. The publication is owned by Oilprice.com, which states it owns shares of REalloys and has an incentive to see its stock perform well; the article includes forward-looking statements with risks.
items.title: Army's nonbinding deal with REalloys for heavy rare earth processing at Tooele

items.summary: Nuclear recycling startup Project Omega has submitted a letter of intent to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, signaling its plan to file a full application within the next few years. The company is attempting to commercialize pyroprocessing technology that would recycle spent fuel into new reactor material while drastically reducing stored waste and hazard. CEO Staff Sheehan said nuclear waste is the industry's biggest challenge and Project Omega exists to reduce both the amount and danger of it. He noted that pyroprocessing cannot separate out pure plutonium, which he called a significant regulatory advantage over aqueous reprocessing used at facilities like La Hague in France or Mayak Production Association in Russia. The company emerged from stealth in February after Sheehan left Air Company, where he developed a process to convert carbon dioxide into hydrocarbons and alcohols for sustainable aviation fuel. Former NRC Chairman Chris Hanson joined as head of implementation. Project Omega has received Department of Energy funding at Idaho National Laboratory, military research with the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, and raised $80 million in a Series A round from Decisive Point venture firm last week. Sheehan said he would pitch his company identically to Democrats or Republicans because he is known as a climate advocate who sticks to his positions. The article also reported on several other stories: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang publicly called for his return as CEO after stepping down amid an extramarital affairs scandal, with the company reporting $116 billion in third quarter revenue; the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers reassessed a permit for EDF Renewables' Atlantic Shores South offshore wind project despite Trump administration promises to ease renewables blockades; General Motors began searching for Mary Barra's successor among internal candidates including Paul Jacobson, Sterling Anderson, and Mark Reuss while developing its standalone battery business; Harvard researchers found grid-connected U.S. data center operations produced more greenhouse gas pollution from May 2024 to April 2025 than Denmark, though the study excluded diesel generators and behind-the-meter power plants; Quaise Energy signed a power purchase agreement with Google for 50 megawatts of electricity from its Project Obsidian superhot geothermal plant expected online by 2030 at about $350 million cost; North America's virtual power plant capacity grew nearly 26% this year to 47.2 gigawatts according to Wood Mackenzie analysis; and the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act faces amendments over National Historic Preservation Act changes affecting tribal sovereignty, with critics arguing the bill sidelines tribes through shorter consultation deadlines while proponents say it enshrines consultation in law.
items.title: Project Omega files NRC letter of intent for nuclear recycling license

items.summary: A reliability watchdog reports that the North American power grid is less at risk of winter blackouts than it was this time last year. The North American Electric Reliability Corp., or NERC, found only three areas are now in an elevated risk category during cold snaps, down from seven a year ago, because there would not be enough reserved capacity to meet peak demand. NERC attributed the improvement to more than 26 gigawatts of new winter peak capacity, driven by about nine gigawatts each of battery storage and gas generation. California and Texas led in deploying storage, while Texas, northern Mexico, and the Mountain West accounted for the largest gas expansions. Emergency orders from the Department of Energy are also helping shore up the grid: they allow operators to direct data centers and other large facilities onto backup generators during peak demand even if it means breaching air pollution limits, and they keep six fossil fuel plants online past their scheduled retirement dates despite raising costs for customers and greenhouse gas emissions. In the United States, only North and South Carolina remain in the elevated risk category amid rapid growth in residential electric heating plus large data centers and industrial loads, which has steadily eroded reserve margins especially during early morning hours before solar generation ramps up. Canadian provinces including Quebec and Nova Scotia are also at elevated risk mainly because gas pipelines are constrained. The assessment arrives as Americans grow concerned about grid reliability; outages are getting longer due to more extreme weather from rising global temperatures, while utilities struggle to modernize fast enough for demand from data centers, reshored manufacturing, and a more electrified economy. Recent nationwide blackout fears spread across social media stemmed from a false manipulated clip of President Donald Trump shared by an account pushing cryptocurrency, per Politifact, with additional anxiety fueled by technology failures affecting air travel, banks, Microsoft, and Apple. Beyond reliability, NERC oversees cybersecurity threats to the bulk power system through mandatory standards for utilities and grid operators aimed at preventing cyber and physical attacks on electric, natural gas, and transmission infrastructure, and serves as the primary hub for sharing sensitive incident data, attack indicators, and vulnerability alerts. In January, NERC said these controls remain critical but are not being updated fast enough to keep pace with changing threats; a major fix would require employees or third-party vendors connecting remotely to smaller energy sites to use two-step login verifications, covering solar, wind, and battery projects as well as substations and fossil fuel plants. Two-step verification is already required of the largest power plants, transmission hubs, and regional control centers. It typically takes several years before updated NERC standards are approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and enforced, and NERC did not reply to a request for comment by publication time.
items.title: North American grid faces fewer winter blackouts, but risks and cyber gaps persist

items.summary: Equinor, Europe's largest pipeline gas supplier, is battling an ongoing cyberattack on its IT systems while European gas prices remain nearly triple last year's level amid the Hormuz crisis. The FBI warned that state-aligned hackers and criminals are using AI-powered tools to breach corporate networks in under three hours. Attacks on energy companies have risen across every measure since 2024, with Check Point recording nearly 70% more attacks on U.S. utilities in the first eight months of 2024 than the same period in 2023, and by May that year U.S. energy firms were fielding about 1,755 attacks a week each. Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups targeting industrial companies in 2025, up from 80 the prior year. Equinor stated on Wednesday it now understands how the attack was carried out and which systems were hit, noting that the attack is not a virus and cannot spread, with no data theft found and no effect on oil and gas output, though restoration timelines remain uncertain. Norway's National Security Authority raised its cyber threat level to the second-highest tier in October after pro-Russian hackers took control of a hydropower dam at Lake Risevatnet in western Norway in April 2025, opening a valve for four hours. Eight months later, Russian state-linked hackers struck Poland's energy system on December 29, 2025, hitting more than 30 wind and solar farms plus a large combined heat-and-power plant, damaging remote terminal units, protection relays and communications equipment; CERT Polska attributed it to the group Berserk Bear while ESET and Dragos linked it to Sandworm. In December 2025, 26 Western security agencies warned that Cyber Army of Russia Reborn, NoName057(16), Z-Pentest and Sector16 had breached poorly secured industrial equipment in energy, water and food sectors across the West; the U.S. Justice Department says the Kremlin funded Cyber Army of Russia Reborn's DDoS-for-hire subscriptions, and Sector16 member Artem Revenskii agreed to plead guilty in California over attacks on oil and gas infrastructure in the United States, Ukraine, Germany, France and Latvia after investigators found messages discussing deforming pipelines. Since April, Iranian state hackers have targeted internet-connected controllers made by Rockwell, Siemens and Schneider Electric at U.S. water and energy providers, with one provider's controller logic rewritten to disable shutdown and alarm functions; suspected Iran-linked hackers also breached tank gauges at gas stations in several states, altering fuel readings per CNN, and were suspected in a four-day British power plant shutdown in July. Iran works through criminal hackers as well: the group Pioneer Kitten handed network access to ransomware gangs for a share of ransoms, with Pay2Key raising affiliates' shares from 70% to 80% for attacks on the United States and Israel, described by KELA as Iran outsourcing geopolitical retribution. Criminal groups have also targeted energy firms for profit: Qilin claimed nearly a terabyte of data from Romania's oil pipeline operator Conpet in February without affecting transport, Gentlemen encrypted systems at Oltenia Energy Complex in December 2025, and TrendAI researchers found a German renewable firm's internal database listed for about $748,000 on criminal forums. The IMF warned that AI is making cyberattacks cheaper, faster and more dangerous; the FBI said ARTEX has been used since at least August against energy and nine other sectors, while Google reported hackers using AI agents to find flaws, write exploits and launch them without human involvement for the first time observed in August, when attackers also used AI-generated scripts targeting Siemens controllers. The damage so far relies on old weaknesses: weak or default passwords accounted for 26% of Dragos' findings at oil and gas companies last year, internet-facing systems for another 26%, and poor separation between business and control networks for 29%. Brian Proctor noted that the barrier once requiring expertise is now time, which is shrinking. Equinor remains working with Norway's national security authorities to contain an attack whose source it has not named.
items.title: Equinor Cyberattack Amid Rising Energy Sector Threats

items.summary: Anthropic, an artificial intelligence firm based in San Francisco that did not exist five years ago, is preparing to ring the opening bell at the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The debut is priced at $83 per share and carries a valuation that eclipses the combined market capitalization of India's ten largest companies. Uday Kotak, Founder and Director of Kotak Mahindra Bank, took to X (formerly Twitter) to highlight what he described as a stark valuation gap between Silicon Valley's AI boom and Indian equities, noting that Anthropic did not exist five years ago.
items.title: Uday Kotak flags valuation gap as Anthropic prepares Nasdaq IPO

items.summary: At Nvidia's first all-hands meeting since founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned, interim CEO Colette Kress addressed employees with the message "let's move forward," according to CNBC reporting that cited attendees present at the roughly one-hour session. The company also announced early pay increases for staff. The meeting was held in person and streamed via Microsoft Teams. It took place a day after Huang offered to return as CEO if the board chose to accept his offer, though he had already stepped down following allegations of at least two affairs. Kress, Nvidia's finance chief, was named interim leader in connection with that departure.
items.title: Nvidia's interim CEO reassures staff amid Jensen Huang departure

items.summary:
Anthropic closed its initial public offering on Wednesday (Nov 18) with a price of US$83 per share, above the range it had targeted and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion. The deal raised US$81.31 billion through an upsized issue of about 980 million shares, roughly 19 per cent more than its original plan to sell 825 million shares between US$70 and US$78 apiece. It also raised US$26 billion in a private placement at the IPO price. On a fully diluted basis the valuation is about US$1.5 trillion, including stock options and restricted stock; on a non-diluted basis it stands at about US$1.1 trillion. The offering made Anthropic the largest stock-market debut on record, surpassing SpaceX's earlier deal, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters in a 22-bank syndicate. Shares are expected to begin trading on Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker ANT.

The IPO followed a roadshow that drew demand several times the number of shares offered, even amid questions about Anthropic's outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as AI competition intensifies. The company is the first major frontier artificial-intelligence model developer to go public, following SpaceX's June offering, while OpenAI is also expected to pursue a listing as early as next year.

Anthropic's growth has been driven by demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code among software developers. Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up about US$10 billion from Sep 30. It reported 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in trailing-12-month revenue as of Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 a year earlier.

Sustaining that growth is proving costly. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, roughly four times the prior-year amount, plus an additional US$5 billion in third-quarter costs, which reduced revenue per dollar of compute. Revenue rose 47 per cent to US$16.96 billion in the third quarter from the second quarter. Operating income turned into a loss of US$567 million after operating profit of US$974 million the prior quarter, while net loss narrowed to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion earlier, partly due to convertible bonds.

The company has committed nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google. Its prospectus warned that some providers depend on third-party financing or credit support for chips and capacity, so if such support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity could be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered. Investors have grown concerned about debt-fueled AI infrastructure expansion.

Anthropic also faces questions over balancing commercial ambitions with its emphasis on safety; CEO Dario Amodei has urged the industry to slow model development and release, warning advances may outstrip society's ability to manage risks. The company said it is considering tighter human oversight of some research decisions as models take on more work.

Competition is intensifying: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by Ramp in September, versus about 8 per cent for Anthropic's Claude Fable. OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate passed US$40 billion in July, though Anthropic led at the time. A Capgemini study found 59 per cent of executives at large companies plan to increase use of open-weight models over the next year as AI costs exceed budgets, and Meta has reportedly reduced its reliance on Anthropic's models while building internal capabilities.

Peter Singlehurst, head of private companies at Baillie Gifford, which invested roughly US$1.5 billion before the IPO, said his bet is that value will accrue to whoever stays at the frontier, arguing Anthropic arguably has the highest probability of remaining there. The prospectus also warned models could develop capabilities faster than the company can evaluate them and put safeguards in place, increasing harm risk; Anthropic noted it may increase human oversight as models take on more work.
items.title: Anthropic completes record $81 billion IPO at ~$1.5 trillion valuation

items.summary: Nvidia's shares dipped Wednesday even as the company reported strong earnings, because investors remained uneasy about the departure of CEO Jensen Huang. The stock decline reflected lingering concerns that leadership instability could trigger a talent exodus and undermine confidence in the chipmaker's direction. To address skepticism among employees and investors alike, Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress initiated what has been described as a charm offensive during the company's first employee town hall since Huang's ouster. In addition to expanding stock buybacks, Kress reportedly promised pay raises at that meeting, while also assuring staff that the firm's "passion to innovate" would remain unchanged. The leadership transition has exposed a notable divide between Silicon Valley and Washington: according to a former politico-turned-tech executive speaking with Semafor's Liz Hoffman, observers outside of politics focus on whether Huang will return to Nvidia by Christmas, whereas in Washington the concern centers instead on whether he faces imprisonment.
items.title: Nvidia Shares Fall Despite Strong Earnings Amid Jensen Huang Departure Uncertainty

items.summary: On Wednesday, Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the price range it had initially set for the debut. The higher-than-expected valuation signals strong investor enthusiasm for what is being described as the first frontier AI lab to go public, even amid recent turmoil in tech stocks following a Democratic sweep in midterms and Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia CEO. Analysts note that investors appear to treat Anthropic as a pure-play AI company, distinguishing it at a time when sentiment toward AI infrastructure and hardware is cooling. The debut could attract roughly $250 million in net retail buying, potentially double SpaceX's record of $118 million in retail purchases.
items.title: Anthropic prices IPO above target range

items.summary: Worldwide equities declined on Wednesday, November 18, after Nvidia's quarterly report and ahead of Anthropic's planned market debut. The fall was compounded by a stronger US dollar driven by comments from Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller, who told CNBC that the central bank must either approve a half-point rate hike at its December meeting or signal a faster pace of hikes in 2027. Mining stocks weighed on European shares, while Nvidia's results initially lifted Asian markets with South Korea's Kospi up 2 per cent overnight; however, the rally faded and Nvidia fell 2.9 per cent after rising as much as 2.7 per cent. Nvidia's board rejected rehiring former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week, leaving uncertainty unresolved. Neil Shah of Counterpoint noted that Tuesday's results had stabilized sentiment and put a floor under the recent AI selloff but postponed rather than permanently cured investor anxiety. In US markets, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.11 per cent to 50,198.17, the S&P 500 lost 0.23 per cent to 7,323.63, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.42 per cent to 24,429.89. The MSCI global gauge fell 0.45 per cent to 1,074.61, while Europe's STOXX 600 dropped 1.03 per cent and emerging market stocks slipped 0.2 per cent; Japan's Nikkei rose 0.28 per cent to 59,024.28. The dollar index climbed 0.17 per cent to a fresh 19-month high of 103.79, with the euro down 0.22 per cent at $1.0973. Juan Perez of Monex USA said traders believe the Federal Reserve is determined to hike rates and possibly do so aggressively, which was carrying the dollar higher. Crude prices fell after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, adding supply-surplus expectations: US crude lost 3.3 per cent to $83.17 a barrel while Brent dropped 1.4 per cent to $91.84 a barrel. Spot gold declined 3.24 per cent to $3,725.10 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.98 per cent to $45.04 an ounce; copper slipped 4.54 per cent to $12,626.00 a ton. Yields on 2-year US Treasury notes edged higher by 1.31 basis points to 4.802 per cent as hawkish Fed comments and minutes from the last policy meeting underscored inflation concerns, while the benchmark 10-year note yield fell 3.47 basis points to 5.068 per cent.
items.title: Global stocks slip on Nvidia results and hawkish Fed as dollar hits fresh high

items.summary: A former McDonald's worker named Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023 and is now 22, has called on the firm to change how it treats younger employees. She says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers during a night shift, telling her to "just suck it up and deal with it." Hope also reported seeing older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers and discussing wanting to sleep with them once they turned 18. She described the branch as having a very sexualised, toxic environment, recounting an incident in which a manager put his hands on her shoulders from behind, after which she said she "moved quick" whenever he approached. Her main concern was for younger teenagers, whom she says were not being looked after and who appeared to be waiting for their 18th birthdays under what she described as a toxic culture where the feeling prevailed that it was no longer illegal because they had aged out of child status. Hope said "That is literally a child still." She joined hundreds of current and former workers bringing discrimination claims against McDonald's, which are being presented by law firm Leigh Day. This week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can proceed to a full hearing expected in April; the BBC understands these relate to indirect discrimination rather than sexual harassment. Hope said she was not taking part for money and hoped the case would change how McDonald's treats allegations, shake up its internal process, make life easier for young people starting their first jobs, and improve safety. She accused the company of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have claims struck out, which Judge Glennie rejected. A McDonald's spokesperson declined to comment on ongoing legal proceedings but said the company had embedded robust safeguarding initiatives as part of its commitment to staff, that any harassment or discrimination is unacceptable, and that it has industry-leading measures in place with external experts.
items.title: McDonald's workers bring discrimination claims over sexualised workplace

items.summary:
The UK faces an emerging risk to gas security, according to a fresh update from the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which says that the danger of insufficient gas during a cold snap remains and calls for an enduring solution. Neso's report stated: "Our updated analysis shows that the risk identified in our 2025 assessment remains, and that there is an ongoing need for an enduring solution to secure future gas supply." Even with new North Sea production such as Jackdaw flowing into the national network this week, the UK will still depend on imports. Possible remedies include additional import terminals, interconnecting pipes to the continent, or reliable domestic gas storage, possibly in combination.

On the storage front, events are moving faster than government decision-making. Centrica has not been filling Rough, the largest offshore storage facility, and will close it next spring unless a deal is reached with the government. Meanwhile, fellow FTSE 100 firm SSE says it is preparing to begin closing its Atwick facility near Hornsea in East Yorkshire, which represents about 20% of Great Britain's onshore gas storage. Both firms are acting rationally from a commercial standpoint: the economics of gas storage depend on summer prices being reliably lower than winter ones to secure a profit margin. In an increasingly global liquefied natural gas market those spreads have disappeared, and geopolitical factors such as the closure of the strait of Hormuz can further complicate matters.

While Atwick could probably be reopened after closure, that is less true of Rough. The government's position has not moved since summer, when it conceded for the first time that intervention may be necessary. An energy department statement repeated: "We recently confirmed plans to explore commercial support for storage and the wider sector, to help protect our gas security." It added that proposals would be set out in due course.

The article argues this is leaving things late. Belt-and-braces gas security for winter already required an eleventh-hour deal with Belgium to avert a planned cut in interconnector capacity. Delay has reportedly handed negotiating clout to the operators if ministers ultimately need to strike a deal, and the storage question cannot wait much longer.

The article notes that the security problem has been recognised for years, even before the first Neso report, yet successive governments have taken remarkably long to assemble a strategy while urging households to stockpile gas. It concludes that it is time for a plan before further facilities close and narrow options.
items.title: UK Gas Storage at Risk as Facilities Close Amid Delayed Government Plan

items.summary: Following a May 2026 government overhaul of private renting that abolished no-fault evictions and moved tenancies onto rolling contracts, the government has acknowledged that deposit protection remains unresolved for many tenants. While reforms are promised and consulting is underway on scrapping insured deposit schemes, the timing of these changes has not yet been confirmed. Housing and planning minister Matthew Pennycook said landlords and letting agents remain permitted to hold tenant deposits in their own bank accounts, creating a power imbalance. The government is now seeking firsthand accounts from private tenants about their experiences with the rental deposit system in England, asking whether they struggled to recover their deposit, whether it was withheld or subject to deductions for damage, and how long disputes took to resolve.
items.title: England private renters invited to report deposit protection struggles

items.summary: The United States and China, described as the world's two largest economies, have agreed to build a constructive strategic stability relationship grounded in respect, fairness, and reciprocity, with cooperation as its main theme. The article frames trade as one of the most measurable forms of that cooperation. According to figures presented for the period from 2001 to 2025, US goods exports to China grew by 454.2%, a figure more than double the 198.6% growth in US exports to the rest of the world over the same span. In 2025, China ranked as the largest export market for US soybeans, the second-largest for integrated circuits, and the third-largest for medical devices. The article also notes that the United States was the largest contributor to China's services trade deficit. These figures are presented by the source as reflecting the mutually beneficial nature of economic ties between the two countries.
items.title: US-China Trade Figures Highlight Economic Interdependence

items.summary: China's Ministry of Commerce announced on Wednesday that China and the Republic of Korea (ROK) have substantially concluded the second phase of negotiations on their Free Trade Agreement. A ministry official stated in response to a media query that this outcome will create new opportunities for enterprises in both countries, consolidate the foundation of bilateral economic and trade cooperation, and inject fresh impetus into the steady development of the China-ROK strategic cooperative partnership. The official also framed the achievement as a pragmatic measure by both sides to uphold multilateralism and free trade while opposing unilateralism and protectionism and safeguarding the multilateral trading system. The second phase upgraded the investment, trade in services, financial services, and economic cooperation chapters along with related annexes of the original agreement. Officials noted these upgrades will expand and improve China-ROK investment and trade in services, strengthen bilateral economic and trade relations, and achieve higher-level mutually beneficial outcomes. Based on this substantial conclusion, both sides are preparing for the formal signing of the upgraded agreement. The FTA was originally signed on June 1, 2015, and entered into force on December 20, 2015. According to China's official statistics, China-ROK trade reached $331.24 billion in 2025, with bilateral trade standing at $440.9 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, surging by 63.7% year on year.
items.title: China-ROK FTA Second Phase Negotiations Concluded

items.summary: Following a Monday (Nov 16) announcement that the United States would tighten exports of advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Brazil on suspicion these countries could serve as routes for diverting chips to China, Indonesia is reviewing the measure's impact. The new rules require companies to obtain US government licences to export, re-export or transfer certain advanced AI chips to the five affected countries, and also apply to overseas data centres that supply large computing capacity to firms headquartered in China, Russia, Iran, Cuba and other nations subject to US controls. Indonesia's Government Communications Agency (GCA) said on Wednesday (Nov 18) it is seeking industry input on how the restrictions affect operations and investment, including in the data centre sector, while remaining open to technical dialogue with counterparts to clarify application and support continued access to advanced computing for legitimate commercial use. M Habib Abiyan Dzakwan of CSIS Indonesia warned that investors from Western countries would grow more cautious, noting that firms previously had only needed to comply with Indonesian regulations but now must also satisfy US requirements; he added the restrictions might not drive investment away entirely but could complicate AI and data centre investments through additional regulatory burdens. Dyah Ayu of CELIOS cautioned that investors may wait for greater clarity on licensing rules, postpone final decisions or build capacity gradually before committing further to AI hardware spending. Citing figures from the Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs, the GCA reported Indonesia's semiconductor device and electronic integrated circuit exports reached approximately US$ 4.1 billion in 2025, up from US$1.5 billion in 2024. Habib suggested the government examine AI chip import data to gauge volumes, sectors involved and operating data centres, which could help address US diversion concerns, while also coordinating with Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand on their responses and strengthening enforcement against illegal diversion. Maria Monica Wihardja of ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute noted that Indonesia is the only affected Southeast Asian country without a dedicated strategic trade management framework, relying instead on a patchwork of customs, import-export and sector-specific regulations; she warned this absence weakens export controls by allowing imported goods to be loosely re-exported elsewhere with unclear legal consequences. Dyah emphasized a deeper risk: domestic operators may struggle to build their own capacity and become mere customers of global providers, increasing Indonesia's dependence on foreign technology as a consumer. The GCA said it is developing a framework to facilitate legitimate trade while reducing the risk of dual-use goods being diverted or misused, reflecting its commitment to an open, predictable and trusted environment and supporting President Prabowo Subianto's direction to develop the semiconductor industry and strengthen Indonesia's role in global supply chains.
items.title: Indonesia reviews US AI chip export curbs amid analyst warnings

items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping stated on Thursday that China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation. He made the remarks at the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting held in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. Xi added that China is ready to work with all parties to build the pillars supporting an Asia-Pacific community.
items.title: Xi positions China as leader of APEC cooperation

items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for continued efforts to build an Asia-Pacific community characterized by solidarity and mutual assistance, openness and integration, and innovation and inclusive development. He made the remarks at the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province. Xi urged strengthening shared interests, working together to address difficulties and challenges, and fostering a sense of community among regional parties. He emphasized the importance of innovation in building this community, calling for encouragement of science and technology exchanges and cooperation, facilitation of the use of innovation outcomes, and cultivation of an open, fair, just, and non-discriminatory environment for cooperation. Xi also stressed upholding openness and integration by advancing economic integration steadily across the Asia-Pacific region. He called on all parties to promote free and open trade and investment, remove bottlenecks in factor flows, and ensure smooth economic circulation throughout the region.
items.title: Xi Jinping Calls for Further Efforts to Build an Asia-Pacific Community

items.summary: In a double murder trial before Justice Natalie Adams, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC told the court that Beau Lamarre-Condon's "wounded pride" after his breakup with Jesse Baird led him to plan revenge. The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his partner Luke Davies at Baird's Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024, using a police Glock while disguised as an Uber Eats driver. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter, with the trial entering its ninth week. Hatfield argued that Lamarre-Condon was infatuated, obsessed and insecure about his relationship with Baird from late 2022 when they began casually dating, pointing to testimony from friends who said he watched Baird have sex with other men, broke into his home for his phone and followed him in a car. Hatfield called this "classic stalking" and described the subsequent break-in as astonishing conduct for a serving officer driven by sexual jealousy. The prosecution argued that after Baird ended things for good in November 2023, Lamarre-Condon wanted to harm him and devised the plan to enter his home disguised as an Uber Eats driver. The defence contends both men died in struggles while Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence, claiming he aimed only at Baird's shoulder to make him drop a knife before accidentally firing twice as they fell. Hatfield countered that forensic evidence shows the first shot struck Baird in the back as he fled toward the rear door and that the near-vertical bullet trajectory through the floor indicates a controlled, execution-style shot to the temple. He argued the timing between shots allowed only two to three steps rather than the wrestling described by Lamarre-Condon, and that Davies was killed by a bullet passing through the door into his head, evidenced by gunshot stippling on the door but not the body. Hatfield noted that key elements of the defence case came solely from Lamarre-Condon's own testimony, with nothing independent to support them.The trial continues.
items.title: Crown alleges wounded pride drove Lamarre-Condon to murder Baird and Davies

items.summary: Bernard Kearney, director of BK Labour Hire, continued his evidence on Thursday before the royal commission investigating alleged corruption in Victoria's construction sector. The company held an enterprise bargaining agreement with the CFMEU that helped it secure lucrative contracts on Big Build projects from around 2022. In September 2025, industry regulator the Labour Hire Authority scrutinized BK Labour over cash withdrawals totalling $77,970 and transfers to entities in the name of former senior CFMEU organiser Joe Myles, totalling $127,472. Rather than provide a statutory declaration explaining those transactions as requested, Kearney admitted he had asked for fake invoices to be created. The fabricated invoices covered sponsorships worth thousands of dollars to the Kangaroos Junior football club, Parkdale Vultures football and netball club, Yarra Jets Junior football club, and Port Melbourne bowling club. Kearney maintained that Myles was paid through his companies for work performed, describing him as an asset for knowledge on health and safety procedures. When asked why he had not simply told the Labour Hire Authority this himself, Kearney replied that he could not answer. The commission heard Wednesday that BK Labour received a succession of invoices from Myles totalling $256,000 over about a year; Myles was sacked by the union in mid-2024. When shown one fake invoice bearing handwriting, Kearney initially claimed it was his own but admitted under questioning that it was not when asked to demonstrate his handwriting on plain paper. Commissioner Chris Kourakis accused him of deliberately withholding information and suggested he was trying to protect business partner Duane Allen; Kearney denied this. On Wednesday, Kearney was also questioned about $165,000 paid to union-aligned Bandidos gang member Joel Leavitt, whom the company said had provided no work for the firm. Kearney admitted paying it and moving on but could not explain why, while counsel assisting the commission Chris Carr suggested only a couple of possible reasons remained: fear of violence or suppression of information Leavitt held about them; Kearney answered that neither applied. No visual was warranted as the figures are separate transactions rather than comparable values across names.
items.title: BK Labour Hire boss admits to fake sponsorship invoices at Big Build royal commission

items.summary: Cruise operator StarDream Cruises announced on Thursday (Nov 19) that its Star Voyager ship will operate under a three-year seasonal deployment based in Singapore, running through 2029. The arrangement was made in partnership with the Singapore Tourism Board (STB), and is expected to provide travellers with more cruise itineraries across Southeast Asia while attracting regional and international fly-cruise visitors who sail from Singapore. Expanded sailings will carry guests to destinations including Jakarta, Krabi, Phuket, Melaka, Langkawi, Penang, Port Klang in Kuala Lumpur, and Pulau Pangkor. The Star Voyager has a passenger capacity of about 2,000 across more than 970 staterooms, with onboard amenities that include a water park, numerous bars and restaurants, a casino, and a theatre. Michael Goh, president of StarDream Cruises, said in a statement that Singapore has been an important market for the cruise line's operations for more than 30 years, noting that this seasonal deployment builds on its long-standing presence there while contributing to Singapore's growth as a leading regional cruise hub. Jean Ng, assistant chief executive of STB's experience development group, added that the three-year deployment runs alongside Genting Dream's year-round sailings and reflects continued confidence in Singapore as a cruise gateway for travellers discovering Asia.
items.title: StarDream Cruises deploys Star Voyager in three-year seasonal program at Singapore

items.summary: Seven Russian figure skaters have been barred from this week's Finlandia Trophy in Helsinki after Finnish authorities moved to prevent athletes holding Russian passports from entering the country. The Russian Figure Skating Federation announced on Tuesday that these seven competitors, including Olympic pairs medalists Anastasia Mishina and Aleksandr Galliamov, would be unable to travel to Finland as a result of the entry restriction. This development threatens their chances of qualifying for the Grand Prix Final. According to Finnish government statements issued by Monday, Russian citizens holding Schengen visas are now permitted into Finland only for work deemed essential to national interests, with sports explicitly excluded from that allowance.
items.title: Russian Skaters Denied Entry to Finlandia Trophy

items.summary: At the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Chinese leader Xi Jinping greeted Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi with a handshake on Thursday for the second consecutive day. This marked their first face-to-face contact more than a year into a standoff between the two countries. The leaders' initial encounter had taken place at a welcome banquet a day earlier, and they appeared to speak for some length afterward, though the substance of her remarks was not immediately clear. For Japanese officials, even customary diplomatic courtesy such as a handshake had become a matter of suspense, with attention focused on whether Beijing would extend routine protocol to Takaichi. The meeting followed comments made by Takaichi last November regarding possible Japanese military intervention in a Taiwan crisis.
items.title: Takaichi and Xi exchange handshakes at APEC summit amid protocol tensions

items.summary:
A Russian official reports that Ukraine has attacked the Crimean Bridge for the third time in a single week. Sergei Aksyonov, Moscow's appointed head of Crimea, confirmed via Telegram on Thursday morning that traffic was temporarily suspended after another strike and said damage assessment was underway. The bridge had already been hit twice earlier this week, with one attack causing severe damage and part of it collapsing into the water. Ukraine has long targeted the infrastructure because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

The latest news arrives as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for talks in China. Separately, Ukrainian sources issued air raid alerts overnight for districts just outside Kyiv, while at least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday; the regional state administration described that strike as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".

President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November, bringing down a key section of the road. That portion of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed after being brought down by Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a collapse.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before." While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge permanently, recent attempts are described as bringing them closer to destroying its crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading toward the front line. Russian forces have also targeted key crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv recently; strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges, causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system, and some power and water outages.
items.title: Crimean Bridge struck for third time this week, Russian official says

items.summary: NSW One Nation Legislative Council candidate Katherine Deves argued that high rates of welfare use among certain migrant groups justify deep cuts to migration, citing a graph she posted showing working-age welfare recipients by country of birth. In an interview with Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney Mornings, Ms Deves claimed up to 24 per cent of some overseas-born cohorts were on welfare and cited concerns about pressure on the NDIS, health, education, and housing systems. The graph she used shows Sudan, Iraq, and Syria as having the highest rates in Australia and cites Department of Social Services and Bureau of Statistics longitudinal data sets as its source, but does not explain the methodology behind the figures. Peter Whiteford, director of the Social Policy Institute at the Australian National University, told 702 ABC Sydney Mornings that the chart was "very misleading" and described it as "completely wrong," adding that most of the numbers were "puzzling to say the least." During the interview Ms Deves also endorsed fellow NSW One Nation candidate Stuart Bonds over comments at an anti-immigration rally suggesting white Australians are being demographically replaced, which she dismissed as a conspiracy theory. New South Wales Premier Chris Minns called her remarks horrifying and said they demonised Middle Eastern Australians and others who have contributed to the state by starting families, building businesses, and joining communities. Ms Deves was contacted for comment.
items.title: ANU researcher rejects One Nation candidate's migrant welfare graph

items.summary: Fiona, a hippo at Cincinnati Zoo born prematurely in 2017 and named after the Shrek character, has been under round-the-clock medical care for about nine days after swallowing a knitted hat. According to zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley, a child tossed the cap into the air near her enclosure when a ceiling fan caught it and propelled it through a small opening above the viewing window. Initially appearing unharmed, staff noticed Fiona's appetite declining and placed her under constant supervision. She underwent a colonoscopy earlier in the week, but officials are hoping to help her pass the object naturally rather than surgically. Surgery has been ruled out on expert advice that it is not an option for fully grown hippos. To encourage movement through her digestive tract, zoo staff borrowed a vibration plate from a nearby horse farm and have had Fiona stand on it several times daily. They are also keeping her hydrated, administering pain medication, feeding her favourite foods, and offering her the scent of coffee, which she has always liked. Dr Wenninger noted that an ultrasound performed Wednesday gave staff optimism that the hat was beginning to pass through her small intestine, adding that Fiona is large enough for a smallish hat to move through. He said the team can only provide supportive care at this point and may need another procedure in the future. When she was born weighing 13 kilograms, Fiona became the smallest hippo known to survive premature birth, with typical birth weights ranging between 25 and 54kg for the species. The article also references a Washington man who was disembowelled by a hippo protecting her young on an African safari last year, as well as the earlier incident involving gorilla Harambe being shot after a three-year-old boy climbed into his enclosure eight months prior.
items.title: Cincinnati Zoo Hippo Fiona Undergoes Treatment After Swallowing a Hat

items.summary: At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, Vanuatu's Environment Minister Ralph Regenvanu called for reform of the UN climate summit process as talks entered their final days. He accused a small group of states of blocking progress at both climate summits and other multilateral negotiations, including the plastics treaty that began under the UN in 2022 but has yet to make progress. The COP operates by consensus, though some countries such as Panama are pushing for majority voting to break deadlocks. Regenvanu named specific blockers: "the Arab bloc and the LMDCs," which he described as a group of around twenty developing countries including Saudi Arabia and India, plus Russia. He also cited US President Donald Trump's withdrawal from climate negotiations, noting that the United States is again absent this year, while acknowledging multiple geopolitical tensions affecting discussions in Antalya. Regenvanu leads Vanuatu's negotiations on climate issues, over a plastics treaty, and at the International Court of Justice, where Vanuatu secured an advisory opinion on climate last year. He acknowledged a deep gap between developed and developing countries on finance but said vulnerable nations must try to build bridges. As part of the Alliance of Small Island States, whose members face rising sea levels and intensifying storms, Regenvanu warned there is a real risk that COP31 could reverse previously agreed commitments as issues thought settled return to the table.
items.title: Vanuatu Minister Calls for UN Climate Summit Reform Amid Backsliding Fears

items.summary: CGTN's First Voice editorial argues that Chinese President Xi Jinping's keynote at the opening of the APEC CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen was fundamentally a defense of economic openness against an era defined by tariffs, industrial policy and geopolitical rivalry. The column characterizes his message as reassurance to Asia-Pacific economies: support free and open trade and investment, maintain smooth global supply chains, and advance the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific. It contends that this language addresses companies facing trade fragmentation as a business risk, which experience geopolitics through higher compliance costs, delayed shipments, duplicated suppliers, uncertain market access and postponed investment decisions rather than abstract theory.
